## 286. Early warnings before a break beyond: T6 checked against the literature (EW1)

```text
Result(s): none new about the unfolding; no record changed; no simulation built. Reuses Web.break_not_bounded,
       Flow.policy_uses_after_failure, Web.observed_raise_couples (Becoming.Runaway) as T6's proved half, and
       section 284's T6 entry.
Delta: thesis T6 corrected (chapter, EN and ZH). The uncoupled side holds by construction where the stock's own
       course is matched and the dependent does not feed back; its first wording fails against controls with
       no rising draw wherever the stock's rate of return falls as it is drawn down, which known theory, a known
       experiment and a field case show. Warnings follow the observed condition's own rate of return (a fold or
```

**What was asked.** The brief asked for a frozen test of T6's untested side. As section 284 left it, T6 said that statistical early warnings come before a break only where the break is a fold of the observed condition's own renewal. Where a drawn stock with no fold of its own crosses a dependent's need, no statistic of the stock's series was to warn more often than in matched series with no break. The design was matched pairs of stochastic stocks under a slowly rising draw (a depensation class, and a compensatory class crossing a dependent's need), predictions frozen before any run. A literature check came first, with a stop rule if the side was already settled.

**What the check found.** The answer turns on what "matched" holds fixed. Matched in the stock's own course (same renewal, same draw, the need crossed in one run and not the other), with a dependent that takes nothing measurable from the stock, the need enters nothing the stock's law depends on. Every statistic then has the same law with and without the break. That is `Web.break_not_bounded` read statistically, and Dekker, von der Heydt and Dijkstra (2018) show the analogue numerically in a one-way cascade. Matched against controls with no rising draw, the standard experimental design, the first wording fails. A stock's lag-1 autocorrelation is about exp(−λΔt) at its rate of return λ. Under a proportional draw e, logistic renewal has λ = r − e = r·x*/K, so the rate of return falls in proportion to the level. Autocorrelation has risen against controls by the time the level crosses any need on the way, and the need itself has no part in this. Kéfi et al. (2013) show slowing down before a transcritical end and a smooth decline. Drake and Griffen (2010) observed it in *Daphnia* crossing a transcritical point, with none in constant controls. Clements et al. (2017) found warnings decades before the collapse of whale stocks under whaling. Whether a stock has a fold of its own also depends on the draw. Under a standing draw, any renewal that peaks has a fold at the largest sustained draw (the regime's point of no return, `Becoming.RegimeMargin`). Only renewal that rises as the level falls (inflow-type) has neither a fold nor a falling rate of return, and only there does the first wording hold against unmatched controls.

**Why it stopped.** Under either matching the simulation's verdict was fixed before it ran. Matched in course, it passes by construction and could fail only through its code. Against unmatched controls, the modeller's choice of renewal decides it: logistic fails, inflow-type passes. A frozen test is worth its freeze only where it can fail on something the tester did not choose. For T6's uncoupled side that is whether actual dependents leave their stock's dynamics unchanged as they near their needs, which only data on actual dependents can show. The brief's stop rule applied; building the simulation would have presented a demonstration as a test.

**What changed in T6.** The claim now says what a statistical warning reads: the observed condition's own rate of return. That rate falls near a bifurcation of its own renewal (a fold, or a transcritical end) and with the level of a compensatory stock under a proportional draw. Before a dependent's break the stock's statistics rise exactly as before the same drawdown with no break; they read the decline, never where the need lies. *Forbids* is stated given the stock's own course, with negligible feedback. *Refuted by* compares against periods of the same stock at the same level with no break. The evidence adds Dai, Korolev and Gore 2015 (the margin must couple into the rate of return even at one's own fold), Boerlijst et al. 2013 (the warning lies in what carries the critical mode, not in what breaks) and Dekker et al. 2018. It records the first wording as failed, with the results that refute it, and says why no simulation was built. The heading is unchanged: "a break is seen coming only through what couples into what breaks" survives the correction. What couples into the observed rate of return is the stock's own level, so the stock's decline is seen coming; the need is not.

**Self-review.** Two judgments could be wrong. First, calling the matched-in-course reading "by construction" assumes the dependent takes no measurable share of the stock and does not change its renewal. Most actual dependents feed back somewhat (a predator eats what it depends on), and then the dependent's approach to its need can show in the stock in proportion to the stock's loading on the dependent's critical mode. That case is T6's coupled side, and the corrected entry scopes the uncoupled side to negligible feedback. Second, the failure of the first wording rests on a derivation and on results for a stock's own end (Drake and Griffen; Kéfi et al.), not on a measured dependent's break. That a dependent's need on the way inherits the stock's rising autocorrelation follows because the indicator is a function of the stock's series alone, which is the same fact that makes the other reading hold by construction. The field test the check points to (Cury et al. 2011's seabirds, whose need is measured on themselves, against their forage-fish series) is open and not claimed here.
